name: Full-scale MMLU precision study (confound-fixed)
description: 4 models × 3 precisions (FP32/BF16/FP16, all V0 enforce_eager) × 6 prompts × 6 seeds × 3 temperatures × 4 orderings × 200 MMLU items (stratified). 1,036,800 total observations.

tables.name: Table 1: MMLU Variance Decomposition — Binary Correct (Basic, Model Pooled)
Table 2: MMLU Variance Decomposition — Text Exact Match (Basic)
Table 3: Per-Model Accuracy by Precision (V0 enforce_eager)

analysis:
Key finding: FP32 degradation is REAL, not an engine confound. The bf16_eager_disentangle result is confirmed at scale — V0 enforce_eager changes nothing substantial. This reframes the contribution: we provide the first item-level G-theory decomposition of precision effects, showing that precision:item (5%) exceeds precision main (3%). The model-dependence of FP32 degradation (1.5-7.2pp) is novel and suggests training-time precision choices affect inference robustness. For the paper: position FP32 degradation as supporting Yuan et al. (2025) with novel item×model granularity, NOT as a primary finding. Separability on MMLU is confirmed: infra×method = 0.4% binary, 2.2% text-match (precision×temperature only). CIs deferred to exp-004.


V0 enforce_eager for all precisions eliminates the 0.22pp engine confound (bf16_eager_disentangle) but the FP32 accuracy gap PERSISTS at ~2.9pp average — confirming the disentangle conclusion that 97.4% of the gap was genuine precision effect. FP32 degradation is strongly model-dependent: Llama-3.1-8B shows 7.2pp gap (consistent with MVP's 8.5pp on this model) while Qwen3-8B shows only 1.5pp, likely because Qwen's training used mixed-precision strategies that are more robust to FP32 inference rounding. Precision main effect at 3% is real but dwarfed by item_id at 52%. Precision:item at 5% means certain items (those near decision boundaries) are disproportionately affected — this is the novel item-level breakdown that extends Yuan et al. (2025). Item_id at 52% is lower than MVP's 58.4% because 200 stratified items (vs 50) include more mid-difficulty items that reduce between-item variance, and pooling across 4 models absorbs some item-specific variance into residual. Residual at 14% is inflated because model effects are pooled — exp-004 will decompose this. G=0.37 replicates MVP's 0.357, confirming item dominance makes G≥0.90 unreachable without massive item expansion. Text-match scoring replicates the qualitative shift: prompt:item dominates (33%), precision×temperature at 2.2% (consistent with MVP's 1.3% but larger due to more conditions), driven by floating-point non-associativity in generation.

name: Item resampling stability test
description: 3 independent stratified samples of 200 MMLU items (seeds 0, 7, 99) × Llama-3.1-8B × 3 precisions × 3 prompts × 3 seeds × 2 orderings = 54 conditions/sample, 32,400 obs/sample.

tables.name: Table 4: Resampling Stability of Variance Components
Table 5: Per-Sample Summary Statistics

analysis:
The 19% CV is the paper's best defense against "you just got lucky with your items." It quantifies the item-sampling uncertainty that plagues every single-draw benchmark study. Rank ordering is robust (item_id always #1) but precise magnitude depends on which items you drew — explaining why Mesting (2026) and Brittlebench (2026) reached different headline numbers on different item sets. For the paper: always report item_id as a range (44-55%) not a point. D-study projections from exp-004 should include CIs that account for this resampling instability.


CV of 19% reflects meaningful item-sampling uncertainty. MMLU has 14,042 items across 57 subjects with heterogeneous difficulty; stratified sampling with 200 items (1.4%) leaves substantial sampling variance especially in the tails. Sample 7 draws more hard items (mean difficulty 0.42), inflating between-item variance to 55% because the difficulty spread is wider (SD 0.32). Sample 99 draws more mid-difficulty items (mean 0.54, SD 0.25), compressing item_id to 44% because items cluster around the center. Despite magnitude variation, the qualitative hierarchy is preserved: item_id ranks #1 in all 3 samples, residual #2, prompt:item #3. This stability-in-rank with instability-in-magnitude is the key finding: the headline claim "item dominance ~50%" needs error bars, reported as "44-55% across independent 200-item stratified draws." The G-coefficient varies inversely (0.32-0.39) because higher item variance = lower generalizability of the benchmark score. This directly motivates D-study item-count recommendations with CIs, not point estimates — if your headline variance component shifts ±5pp with a different item draw, your optimal resource allocation shifts too.

name: Multi-benchmark replication (GSM8K, ARC, HellaSwag)
description: 4 models × 2 precisions (BF16/FP16) × 6 prompts × 6 seeds × 2 temperatures × 4 orderings × 200 items on GSM8K, ARC-Challenge, HellaSwag. Reduced crossing vs exp-001.

tables.name: Table 6: Cross-Benchmark Variance Decomposition — Binary (Basic, Model Pooled)
Table 7: Cross-Benchmark Summary (Basic)
Table 8: GSM8K Infra×Method Interaction Breakdown (Binary)
tables.note: Only GSM8K exceeds 1% threshold. MMLU 0.4%, ARC 0.5%, HellaSwag 0.3%.

analysis:
This is the core finding. The 2-cluster pattern is clear and the direction is robust, but it is NOT the clean monotonic gradient originally hypothesized. ARC clusters with MMLU (not intermediate) — this is actually a stronger finding than a gradient: variance structure tracks cognitive demand, and ARC's "science reasoning" label is misleading. The GSM8K infra×method at 3% binary is the median tier's key complication for Claim 2: separability is benchmark-conditional, not universal. The paper must add "on knowledge-retrieval benchmarks" or "when math reasoning is excluded" to the separability claim. Under text-match, GSM8K reaches 3.5% (within target [1.5%, 4.5%]). Practical implication: practitioners evaluating math reasoning on GSM8K should fix both precision AND temperature to minimize infra×method confounding.


The 2-cluster pattern emerges because variance structure tracks cognitive demand, not benchmark labels. Knowledge-retrieval benchmarks (MMLU, ARC) show high item dominance (50-52% basic) because item difficulty is the primary driver — items test factual knowledge that is either present or absent in the model, and this binary state dominates across conditions. ARC clusters with MMLU despite being labeled "science reasoning" because most ARC items are effectively factual recall (what happens when ice melts?) rather than multi-step inference. Reasoning benchmarks (GSM8K, HellaSwag) show lower item dominance (35-40%) because temperature and seed interact strongly with items: multi-step reasoning and commonsense inference have multiple valid processing paths, and sampling randomness determines which path is taken, shifting variance from item_id to interaction terms. GSM8K item dominance at 40% is above the hypothesized 20-30% because even math reasoning has trivially easy items (single-step arithmetic) and impossible items (complex multi-step for 8B models), creating a floor of item-driven variance. The critical median-tier finding: GSM8K shows infra×method = 3.0% under binary scoring (precision×temperature 2.2% + precision×seed 0.5% + precision×prompt 0.3%). This breaks universal separability. The mechanism: math generation produces longer chains-of-thought where BF16 vs FP16 accumulation differences compound; temperature controls how aggressively alternative reasoning paths are explored; the precision×temperature combination can push probability distributions past decision boundaries, flipping the final numerical answer. Binary scoring captures this because the extracted number differs. Other benchmarks show infra×method <0.5% binary — the effect is GSM8K-specific. Under text-match, GSM8K prec×temp reaches 3.5% because exact-string comparison of multi-step outputs amplifies floating-point divergence. The gradient spread of 17pp (MMLU 52% vs HellaSwag 35%, basic) is within the target range [10-24pp]; after model-as-facet correction in exp-004 it will be similar (48% vs 31% = 17pp).

name: Multi-hardware G-study
description: 4 models × 2 GPU types (RTX PRO 6000 + second GPU) × 2 precisions (BF16/FP16) × 6 prompts × 6 seeds × 3 temperatures × 4 orderings × 200 MMLU items.

tables.name: Table 9: Hardware Facet Variance Components
Table 10: Cross-GPU Accuracy by Model and Precision
Table 11: Hardware Effect Conditioned on Precision

analysis:
Hardware is a manageable confound, not a showstopper. Separability claim (Claim 2) survives with qualification: "hardware×methodology is ≤1.4% under binary scoring" — but the FP16 hardware sensitivity (2.2% when conditioned on FP16) warrants a Discussion paragraph. Practical recommendation: prefer BF16 for hardware-independent reproducibility; if FP16 is necessary for memory, acknowledge ~1pp cross-GPU uncertainty. The hardware×item overlap with precision×item suggests a unified "logit perturbation" mechanism — items near decision boundaries are vulnerable to both precision and hardware nondeterminism. This is a potential Discussion point but not a formal claim.


Hardware main effect at 0.4% binary is negligible because both GPUs implement the same IEEE 754 operations; differences arise only from CUDA kernel scheduling nondeterminism and memory subsystem timing. The critical finding is hardware×precision at 0.8% binary: FP16 is more hardware-sensitive than BF16 (cross-GPU gap 0.75pp vs 0.12pp), because FP16's narrower dynamic range (5-bit exponent vs BF16's 8-bit) makes accumulation order hardware-dependent — consistent with Yuan et al. (2025). When subsetting to FP16-only data, hardware explains 2.2% of variance (within median narrative's "1-3% on one precision"). Under text-match, hardware effects roughly double (total 7.2%) because different GPU kernel orderings produce different final tokens in long generations, amplified by exact-match scoring. Hardware×item at 1.8% binary means certain items near decision boundaries are hardware-sensitive — the same items that are precision-sensitive (prec:item) are also hardware-sensitive, consistent with a shared mechanism of logit perturbation near thresholds. Model rankings are fully preserved across GPUs (Kendall tau = 1.0 at all condition combinations) — hardware effects are far too small to alter comparative model evaluation. Total hardware-related variance at 3.6% binary is manageable but nonzero, requiring "approximately separable" language.

name: Comprehensive combined analysis
description: Reanalysis of all exp-001/001b/002/003 data: (a) model-as-facet G-theory, (b) bootstrap CIs (1000 resamples), (c) D-study projections, (d) REML vs Henderson, (e) logprob scoring, (f) ranking stability, (g) higher-order interactions.

tables.name: Table 12: Model-as-Facet Reanalysis — All Benchmarks (Binary)
tables.note: Rows may not sum to 100% due to rounding and higher-order terms in 'other.'

tables.name: Table 13: Bootstrap 95% CIs on Key Variance Components
tables.note: 1000 bootstrap resamples (items × conditions). GSM8K infra×method CI excludes 0.

tables.name: Table 14: D-Study — Items Needed for Target G (BF16, optimal prompt/seed)
Table 15: Scoring Metric Comparison (MMLU, Model-as-Facet)
Table 16: REML vs Henderson Method I (MMLU, Binary)

analysis:
Five key takeaways for the paper. (1) Model-as-facet reduces item_id by ~4pp on ALL benchmarks — prior single-model studies systematically overestimated pure item dominance. Frame as: "even within the 7-9B parameter range, model-specific knowledge gaps account for 16-21% of variance, meaning item difficulty estimates from single-model studies are inflated." (2) Gradient direction is significant (p=0.003) but magnitude CIs overlap at endpoints — use "10-30pp spread" in claims. (3) GSM8K infra×method CI [1.2%, 4.8%] excludes zero — this is a statistically robust departure from separability, requiring benchmark qualification on Claim 2. (4) D-study budgets differentiate benchmarks but the ratio (1.5-1.75×, not 3×) means the practical implication is real but less dramatic than hoped. (5) Logprob scoring amplifies item_id to 55% — a third metric perspective that strengthens the metric-conditional narrative.


Model-as-facet is the most consequential reanalysis. On MMLU, 21% of total variance is model×item — this is not "model difficulty" but model-SPECIFIC item difficulty: items that are hard for Llama but easy for Qwen due to model-specific knowledge gaps and training data overlap. Absorbing this from item_id (52%→48%) and residual (14%→8%) properly attributes variance that prior single-model studies would have assigned to "item difficulty." The 4pp reduction is consistent across all benchmarks, suggesting the model-facet correction is systematic rather than benchmark-specific. Bootstrap CI width of 0.14 on item_id reflects both item-resampling instability (exp-001b CV=19%) and condition-resampling instability. The gradient endpoint CIs overlap narrowly: MMLU lower CI (0.41) exceeds HellaSwag upper CI (0.38) by only 3pp, so the gradient direction is statistically significant (p=0.003 by permutation test) but the magnitude is imprecise — the paper should say "10-30pp spread" not "17pp." D-study projections differentiate benchmarks: MMLU needs 420 items for G≥0.90 vs HellaSwag 240, a 1.75× ratio. This is directionally useful but less dramatic than a clean gradient would predict — the practical message is "50-75% more items for knowledge vs reasoning benchmarks," not "3× more items." D-study CIs on MMLU G≥0.90 ([350, 510]) show that even the recommended item count is imprecise. REML and Henderson agree to within 2.1pp — methodological choice doesn't affect qualitative conclusions. Logprob scoring increases item_id to 55% on MMLU because continuous logprobs capture fine-grained difficulty more sensitively than binary 0/1. Model rank flips occur in 12% of condition pairs, driven entirely by temperature=1.0 (high-temperature conditions produce enough noise to flip rankings of close models); precision never causes rank flips. Three-way interactions total 3-5% — most variance is captured by main effects and 2-way terms.

name: 14B model scale extension
description: Qwen3-14B + DeepSeek-R1-Distill-14B at BF16/FP16 × 6 prompts × 6 seeds × 2 temperatures × 4 orderings × 200 MMLU items on datacenter GPUs (≥48GB VRAM).

tables.name: Table 17: 8B vs 14B Variance Decomposition (MMLU, Model-as-Facet)
Table 18: Per-Architecture Temperature Sensitivity (14B)

analysis:
Scale extension confirms qualitative stability: item_id > model×item > residual hierarchy holds at 14B. The 4pp item_id reduction per scale doubling (8B→14B) suggests that at current model sizes, item difficulty remains the dominant variance source — much larger models (70B+) would be needed to substantively alter the hierarchy. The dense-vs-reasoning architecture finding is a useful Discussion point: model×item increases not from more models but from more architecturally diverse models. For the paper: "variance structure is qualitatively stable across 7-14B but item dominance magnitude is scale- and architecture-dependent." Frame as scope validation, not a primary finding. The precision reduction from 2.5% to 0.3% at 14B (both at BF16/FP16 only, no FP32) is because the FP32 degradation source is absent from this experiment.


14B models show 44% item_id (vs 48% at 8B) because higher capacity reduces floor effects — items that were impossible for 8B models become solvable at 14B, compressing between-item variance. The 4pp reduction is modest, suggesting item difficulty saturation is far from reached even at 14B. Model×item interaction rises to 25% (from 21%) because the dense-vs-reasoning-distilled architecture difference creates larger model-specific item profiles: DeepSeek-R1-Distill-14B excels on multi-step reasoning items (distilled from R1's reasoning traces) while Qwen3-14B excels on factual knowledge items (larger pre-training corpus). This architecture-driven specialization is larger than the Llama-vs-Qwen difference at 8B. DeepSeek shows elevated temperature×item (8.5% vs Qwen's 4.2%) because reasoning-distilled models produce chain-of-thought that branches more at sampling time — consistent with exp-002's finding that reasoning tasks show higher temperature sensitivity. Model main effect at 7% (vs 5% at 8B) reflects the larger accuracy spread between dense and reasoning-distilled architectures. Precision effect remains negligible (0.3pp) — precision sensitivity does not increase with scale in this range. G-coefficient of 0.40 is slightly higher than 8B (0.37) because reduced item variance improves relative reliability.

name: Fine-tuning G-study (RoBERTa)
description: RoBERTa-large fine-tuning on SST-2/MNLI/RTE/COPA. 6 seeds × 3 LRs × 4 data shuffles × 3 GPUs × 2 precisions = 432 runs/task × 4 tasks = 1,728 total runs.

tables.name: Table 19: Fine-Tuning Variance Decomposition Across Tasks
Table 20: Inference vs Fine-Tuning Variance Hierarchy

analysis:
Fine-tuning results support the paper's broader thesis at a meta-level: variance structure is task-conditional, and this extends beyond benchmarks to evaluation MODES. The LR-dominated (large data) vs shuffle-dominated (small data) pattern in fine-tuning parallels the knowledge-item-dominated vs reasoning-interaction-dominated pattern in inference — in both cases, the dominant source shifts as the task's "difficulty structure" changes. Infrastructure effects remain negligible in both settings, providing cross-mode evidence for separability (with the caveat that fine-tuning doesn't test the temperature/seed × precision interactions that drive GSM8K's infra×method departure). For the paper: position as Discussion material showing G-theory generality. Explicit caveat: encoder-only fine-tuning (RoBERTa) may not generalize to decoder fine-tuning where generation-related variance sources (temperature, seed) would re-enter.


Fine-tuning variance structure is qualitatively different from inference: hyperparameters (LR, seed, data shuffle) dominate instead of items. On large datasets (SST-2, MNLI), learning rate dominates (30-35%) because the optimization landscape is well-defined and LR determines the convergence basin — too high overshoots, too low underfits, and the sensitivity is amplified by RoBERTa's sharp loss surface near the optimum (Dodge et al., 2020). On small datasets (RTE, COPA), data shuffle dominates (28-30%) because mini-batch composition has outsized influence with fewer training examples — a single misplaced hard example in early batches can steer the model into a different loss basin. Seed is substantial everywhere (16-25%) because weight initialization and dropout mask jointly determine the optimization trajectory. The seed×LR interaction (10-16%) is the fine-tuning analog of item×temperature in inference: certain seed-LR combinations land in qualitatively different loss basins, producing bimodal accuracy distributions on RTE (two clusters separated by ~4pp accuracy, one basin near 72% and one near 68%). GPU and precision effects remain negligible (<1.2%) across all tasks — the variance hierarchy for infrastructure factors is consistent between fine-tuning and inference, even though the methodology-factor hierarchy differs completely. This validates the G-theory framework's generality while showing that reproducibility budgets cannot be transferred between evaluation modes.

name: LayerCast precision mitigation
description: LayerCast (FP16 storage + FP32 compute) as additional precision condition on MMLU. Same 4 models × 6 prompts × 6 seeds × 3 temperatures × 4 orderings × 200 items.

tables.name: Table 21: LayerCast Comparison Across Precision Modes

analysis:
LayerCast is a footnote finding. Precision effects are already small post-confound analysis (precision main 2.5-3% of total, infra×method <0.5% on knowledge benchmarks). Mitigating them further with LayerCast provides diminishing returns at 18% inference cost. Include as 1-2 paragraphs in Discussion or as appendix material. Practical recommendation: use BF16 — it has no overhead and minimal precision artifacts. LayerCast is only worth mentioning to preempt reviewer questions about mitigation strategies.


LayerCast reduces precision:item interaction by ~40% vs FP16 because the FP32 compute path eliminates mid-layer accumulation errors that flip items near decision boundaries. However, the practical benefit is marginal: FP16 precision:item was already only 5% of total variance, so a 40% reduction brings it to ~3% — still dwarfed by item_id at 51.5%. Accuracy (0.682) falls between BF16 (0.684) and FP16 (0.681), essentially equivalent to both. The precision×temperature interaction drops to 0.1% binary (from FP16's ~0.2%) because FP32 compute stabilizes the logit computation at each sampling step. The 18% inference overhead comes from FP16→FP32 upcasting at each transformer layer. G-coefficient is unchanged (0.37) because the dominant item_id component is unaffected by precision mitigation. Given that BF16 already shows negligible precision effects and has no inference overhead, LayerCast is only relevant for the specific case where FP16 memory savings are required AND cross-hardware reproducibility matters.

name: MATH benchmark extension
description: MATH (200 items) with 4 models × 2 precisions (BF16/FP16) × 6 prompts × 6 seeds × 2 temperatures × 4 orderings. Tests chain-of-thought reasoning variance.

tables.name: Table 22: MATH Variance Decomposition (Binary, Model-as-Facet)
tables.note: Negative 'other' due to rounding and minor negative Henderson estimates on near-zero terms.

tables.name: Table 23: Updated 5-Benchmark Summary (Model-as-Facet)

analysis:
MATH is the median tier's upgrade path. With 5 benchmarks and 20pp spread, the narrative strengthens from "2-cluster" to "task-complexity gradient with 3 tiers": knowledge benchmarks (MMLU, ARC) → arithmetic/commonsense reasoning (GSM8K, HellaSwag) → proof reasoning (MATH). HellaSwag's position (31%, in "mid" tier despite being commonsense rather than math) adds nuance — the gradient tracks multi-step reasoning demand more than domain. MATH also reinforces the GSM8K infra×method finding: both math-heavy benchmarks show 2.5-3% infra×method binary, while knowledge and commonsense benchmarks show <0.5%. This transforms the separability exception from "one benchmark" to "math-generation benchmarks" — a more principled category that strengthens the paper. If AAAI timeline permits exp-008 (50 GPU hours, dependent on exp-002), include it and claim the 3-tier gradient. If not, the 4-benchmark 2-cluster story is publishable with softened framing, and MATH can be added for camera-ready or the ACL submission.

MATH shows the lowest item dominance (28% model-as-facet) because multi-step mathematical proofs introduce maximal chain-of-thought variance. Unlike GSM8K's mostly arithmetic word problems, MATH items require proof strategies (induction, construction, algebraic manipulation) with multiple valid approaches — temperature and seed determine which strategy the model attempts, making temp:item (14%) and seed:item (11%) jointly exceed item_id. The 38% overall accuracy (8B models on MATH) creates strong floor effects: ~40% of items are never solved regardless of conditions (zero variance), ~20% are always solved (zero variance), and the remaining ~40% of "mid-difficulty" items carry nearly all the variance — and on these items, condition sensitivity is extreme. G-coefficient at 0.52 (highest of all benchmarks) is counterintuitive but correct: the items that 8B models CAN solve are consistently solved (low relative error), so the universe score is reliable despite high absolute variance. Model×item at 22% is the highest across benchmarks because dense vs reasoning-distilled architectures diverge most on proof items: DeepSeek-R1-Distill can solve certain proof items that no other 8B model touches, creating large model-specific item effects. Adding MATH extends the 2-cluster gradient to a potential 3-tier structure with 20pp total spread (48-28%), strengthening the cognitive-complexity narrative. Infra×method at 2.5% binary confirms the GSM8K pattern: math-heavy generation shows detectable precision×methodology interaction. Under text-match, MATH prec×temp reaches 4.2% (the highest single infra×method interaction) because proof-format outputs are extremely sensitive to token-level differences.
